required_units.text: Space for your own cycle or review record, questions and notes, followed by your treatment card.
Sorafenib: differentiated thyroid cancerNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00294

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Record each review; boxes do not imply a fixed course.
Sorafenib · copy this sheet for another cycle of the same phase.
□ Tiredness improves with rest
□ Rest does not help; usual tasks affected: call
□ Self-care difficult: urgent review
□ Queasy but eating and drinking
□ Intake reduced: contact the team
□ Unable to maintain intake: urgent review
□ Collapse / severe dehydration: 112/999
□ Persistent diarrhoea / constipation: call
□ Blood, severe pain or dehydration: urgent review
□ Collapse or severe sudden illness: 112/999
□ New small change: report
□ Persistent rash / itch: contact team
□ Painful, spreading or blistering rash: urgent review
□ Severe skin reaction with acute illness: emergency help
□ New palpitations: contact team promptly
□ Palpitations with dizziness: urgent assessment
□ Chest pain or fainting: emergency assessment
□ Severe chest pain, collapse or breathing difficulty: 112/999

previous_short_page.text: DECISION, a randomised placebo-controlled study in radioactive-iodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, reported median progression-free survival of 10.8 versus 5.8 months (hazard ratio 0.587; 95% CI 0.454–0.758). unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology urgently for fever, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, persistent vomiting or inability to drink. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure: call 112/999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
This treatment aims to slow cancer growth and help control symptoms. Your team explains the expected benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for your situation.
Sorafenib blocks several enzymes involved in signals that help cancer cells grow and new blood vessels form. It can also affect healthy blood vessels, skin and thyroid hormone control.
What to watch forTell the team before surgery or dental procedures. Report painful palms or soles early; skin care and early dose review can help prevent severe hand-foot reactions.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.
Sorafenib 400 mg twice daily, every day, until progression or unacceptable side effects.
The team reviews the cancer, side effects and your preferences. Scans follow your individual treatment plan; this regimen does not set one universal scan interval.
Use the individual prescription and appointment calendar. No universal tumour-marker panel or scan interval is assumed.
Checks organ safety and suitability before treatment.
Finds changes that may need supportive care, a dose hold or adjustment.
Distinguishes treatment selection, hormone monitoring and cancer response.
Progressive, locally advanced or metastatic differentiated thyroid cancer that no longer responds to radioactive iodine.
Blood and organ safetyNCCP
Full blood count, kidney and liver tests, blood pressure, thyroid tests and assessment of heart function.

Consider blood count, kidney and liver tests at Day 14 of the first month. Repeat these bloods and thyroid tests every 28 days. Check blood pressure weekly in month 1, then every 28 days; check international normalised ratio (blood-clotting test) (INR) as indicated if taking warfarin.
Extra tests may be needed for symptoms, dehydration or abnormal results.
Review results, recovery and previous toxicity before any restart or next dose.
Appointments and medicinesNCCP
Agree the treatment aim, dose and complete medicines list.

Take with water, without food or with a low- or moderate-fat meal. For a high-fat meal, take sorafenib at least 1 hour before or 2 hours afterwards. Follow the prescribed morning and evening doses; never change the dose yourself.
Keep a current dose and symptom record.
Tell the team before surgery or dental procedures. Report painful palms or soles early; skin care and early dose review can help prevent severe hand-foot reactions.
Keep follow-up and recovery checks even after the last dose.
Cancer-specific and specialist testsNCCP
Thyroid tests monitor hormone balance. Thyroglobulin and other response tests depend on the cancer subtype and specialist plan; they are not substitutes for scans.
Confirm the booked test dates with your team.
Safety tests and response tests have different purposes.
Agree the named follow-up team and remaining checks.

Ask / act: Consider blood count, kidney and liver tests at Day 14 of the first month. Repeat these bloods and thyroid tests every 28 days. Check blood pressure weekly in month 1, then every 28 days; check INR as indicated if taking warfarin.

Take with water, without food or with a low- or moderate-fat meal. For a high-fat meal, take sorafenib at least 1 hour before or 2 hours afterwards. Follow the prescribed morning and evening doses; never change the dose yourself. Follow your prescription. A hold or restart must be agreed with the team.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Confirm the next appointment, dose, support medicines and verified daytime and out-of-hours phone numbers.
This is minimal-to-low oral sickness risk; the team agrees rescue medicine if needed.
Follow the unit’s mouth-care plan. Report pain, poor intake or weight loss early; ask for dietetic support. Pace activity, rest and work around symptoms.

Call oncology urgently for fever, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, persistent vomiting or inability to drink. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure: call 112/999.
Bring all prescription, non-prescription and herbal medicines. Check with the oncology pharmacist before starting or stopping anything.

The team reviews the cancer, side effects and your preferences. Scans follow your individual treatment plan; this regimen does not set one universal scan interval. Discuss suitable alternatives, supportive care and the option of declining treatment.
Research supports a treatment discussion; it cannot predict one person’s outcome.

DECISION, a randomised placebo-controlled study in radioactive-iodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, reported median progression-free survival of 10.8 versus 5.8 months (hazard ratio 0.587; 95% CI 0.454–0.758). The cited overall-survival analysis did not show a statistically significant difference. Progression-free survival measures time without progression or death, not a predicted lifespan.

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
